subject: Urban Planning
title: Roman Aqueducts: Engineering an Empire
description: A micro-lesson that makes Roman Aqueducts: Engineering an Empire usable.

hook.text: Rome delivered 300 million gallons of water daily through 11 aqueducts — all powered by gravity alone.

buildup.text: Aqueducts dropped just inches per mile. Engineers calculated the slope so precisely that water flowed uphill through siphons.

discovery.text: The system supplied public fountains every 80 meters. No Roman was ever more than a minute from fresh water.

twist.text: When the aqueducts fell in the 6th century, Rome shrank from 1 million to 30,000 people. No water, no city.

climax.text: Modern cities still use gravity-fed aqueducts. Los Angeles pumps water 240 miles from the Colorado River using the same principle.

punchline.text: No water, no city. Rome proved that 2,000 years ago.

quiz.question: What happened to Rome when its aqueducts were destroyed?
options: The city switched to well water and maintained its population
Population collapsed from 1 million to about 30,000
The military rebuilt them within a decade
